final_answer:
The assistant outlines that merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that recursively splits the list into smaller sublists until each sublist contains a single element (which is inherently sorted). It then merges adjacent sublists into a single sorted list by comparing the front elements of each sublist and appending the smaller one to the result. This merging process continues until the entire list is reconstructed in sorted order. The algorithm operates in O(n log n) time in all cases and has a stable sort property, preserving the relative order of equal elements.

The assistant notes that merge sort is preferred for linked lists over quicksort because of the nature of linked list access. Quicksort typically relies on random access to pivot elements, which is inefficient for linked lists due to their sequential structure. Partitioning in quicksort for linked lists would require additional overhead, such as maintaining pointers or creating auxiliary structures, increasing time complexity and implementation complexity. In contrast, merge sort’s divide-and-conquer approach aligns well with linked lists, as splitting and merging can be done efficiently by traversing nodes, without requiring random access or large contiguous memory blocks. Additionally, merge sort’s worst-case performance (O(n log n)) avoids the risk of quicksort degenerating to O(n²) for unbalanced partitions, making it more predictable for linked lists.
